word:lxx:L700071.explanation: Abioud, also rendered Aviuth, is a personal name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper name when it appears in a sentence. The name occurs 13 times across 13 verses in the LXX corpus, from Exodus through 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific family or historical role cannot be stated here, but its ordinary lexical function is to name a person.

word:lxx:L700224.explanation: This adjective means “adamantine,” describing something associated with adamant and characterized by exceptional hardness or firmness. It is a rare word in the Greek LXX corpus, occurring twice: once in Amos and once in 4 Maccabees. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise descriptive force in each passage cannot be stated more narrowly, but its central idea is hardness, strength, and resistance to yielding.

word:lxx:L700282.explanation: This noun refers to garrulity—excessive, empty, or idle talk. It describes speech marked more by needless words than by useful substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, so it represents a recurring biblical concern about talk that lacks purpose or value. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains speech that is frivolous, wordy, or unhelpful.

word:lxx:L700350.explanation: Azōtisti is a proper name referring to Azotisti. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 13:24. The lexical wording identifies the term as Azōtisti or Azotisti, but no broader definition or verse text is available here to explain its precise role in that occurrence. It belongs to the Greek LXX vocabulary and should remain distinct from Greek New Testament word entities.

word:lxx:L700448.explanation: This adjective describes something that sucks blood or is greedily hungry for blood. It portrays blood-seeking behavior in a sharply negative way, emphasizing an intense and destructive appetite rather than ordinary hunger. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in 4 Maccabees 10:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central meaning remains a blood-sucking or blood-greedy quality.

word:lxx:L700516.explanation: This noun means “thistle,” referring to a prickly plant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 14:9. Its basic meaning identifies a plant rather than an action, quality, or person. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain any figurative or contextual force it may have there; the word itself carries the ordinary sense of a thistle.

word:lxx:L700563.explanation: This adjective describes something that is not shared with another person or group. It can identify something kept apart from participation, fellowship, or common use, though the precise application depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, at Wisdom 14:21. Its basic meaning remains focused on separation from what others share, rather than describing the reason for that separation or the feelings connected with it.

word:lxx:L700642.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “pain,” referring to physical or inward suffering. It names the distress a person experiences rather than an action or command. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including three occurrences in Lamentations, where pain is especially prominent as a human experience. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the experience of pain or anguish.

word:lxx:L700707.explanation: This adjective means “speaking a foreign language.” It describes someone who speaks in a language different from the one normally understood by the listener. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 3:6, so its basic sense is clear even though this word has a very limited occurrence record. Its focus is language difference: the speaker is foreign-language-speaking in relation to those hearing or being addressed.

word:lxx:L700790.explanation: This word is a proper name, appearing as “Ambakoum” or “Amvakum.” It functions as a personal name rather than a description, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs nine times, with occurrences connected to Habakkuk and Bel and the Dragon. The name appears in Habakkuk 1:1 and 3:1 and also in several places in Bel and the Dragon. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse.

word:lxx:L700844.explanation: Ammioud is a personal name, also rendered “Ammiuth.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:4. The available lexical sense is limited to the name itself, so its precise identity and role must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone. This is a Greek LXX name and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament word or as a common vocabulary term.

word:lxx:L700909.explanation: This noun means a rider—a person who rides, especially one mounted on an animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly identifies mounted people rather than the animal itself. The word occurs 24 times across 20 verses, including passages in Exodus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Haggai, and Zechariah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains a mounted rider or group of riders.

word:lxx:L701036.explanation: This noun means “filling up”—the act or condition of being made full or complete. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel, so its meaning is focused rather than broadly illustrated across many books. The word appears in Daniel 9:2 and Daniel 12:13, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force in each passage. Its central idea remains the completion or fullness of something that has been lacking or unfinished.

word:lxx:L701043.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “unfold” or “unroll”—to open something that has been folded or rolled so it lies open. It describes an action rather than an object, and its exact force depends on what is being opened in the surrounding verse. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, including uses in Deuteronomy, Judges, 2 Kings, and Ezekiel. Its clearest English rendering here is “unfold,” while “unroll” expresses the same basic action.

word:lxx:L701115.explanation: This adjective means “immense,” describing something extraordinarily great in size, extent, or scale. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), at 3 Maccabees 1:28. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic sense is clear: it points to something vast or beyond ordinary measure.

word:lxx:L701238.explanation: This verb means “resist”: to stand against something rather than accept or yield to it. It expresses opposition or refusal in action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Deuteronomy and once in Joshua. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains active resistance or standing firm against an opposing force.

word:lxx:L701285.explanation: Anydros means waterless, describing land that is dry and without water.

word:lxx:L701304.explanation: Anōch, also rendered Anokh, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its significance is its role as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament, and the available lexical information does not provide an additional meaning or interpretation for the name itself. This LXX word occurs once, in Joshua 15:43. Understanding what the named reference represents requires the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

word:lxx:L701432.explanation: This verb means “wean”: to bring a nursing child to the point of no longer depending on breast milk. It describes a practical change in a child’s nourishment and care, and its use in the Greek Old Testament is limited to eight occurrences. The word can therefore refer to the completion of nursing, whether spoken of directly in family life or used in a comparison. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L701494.explanation: This noun refers to concealment or a covering—something that hides or shields another thing from view. Its central idea is the act or condition of being covered rather than an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Job and Jeremiah, so it is relatively uncommon. One English rendering is “covering,” which fits its basic sense. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

word:lxx:L701511.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “become petrified”—to become hard or stone-like. It describes a change of condition rather than simply naming a thing. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Exodus 15:16, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the verb.

word:lxx:L701645.explanation: This adverb means “thoughtlessly”: it describes an action done without careful thought or consideration. It tells the reader how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense is acting carelessly instead of with deliberate attention.

word:lxx:L701700.explanation: Arbok is the name of a city.

word:lxx:L701797.explanation: Arour, also rendered Arur, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an idea or action. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, once in Ezra 2:51 and once in Nehemiah 7:53. The available wording identifies the name but does not explain whether it refers to a particular person, family, or place. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding lists and passages in those chapters.

word:lxx:L701818.explanation: This word means “male,” identifying a person or animal as male. It can function either as a noun for a male or as an adjective describing something male. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 53 times, including descriptions of human beings, animals, and sacrificial animals. Its central sense remains consistent across these uses: the male sex, distinguished from the female. The word appears from Genesis through later biblical writings, showing ordinary descriptive use rather than a specialized meaning.

word:lxx:L701937.explanation: This word means “infirmity” or “ailment,” referring to a condition of weakness or sickness. As a noun, it names the condition itself rather than the person who experiences it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages from Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a bodily or personal weakness understood as an ailment or infirmity.

word:lxx:L702028.explanation: Asyberi, also rendered Asiviri, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named individual or designation in the Greek Old Testament, but the available lexical information does not establish more about the person or group named. This LXX form occurs once, in Numbers 26:42. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

word:lxx:L702095.explanation: This adjective means “dishonored”: regarded as lacking honor, respect, or good standing. It describes a person or thing treated as disgraceful, insignificant, or unworthy of esteem. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word is used for conditions of social shame or rejection rather than honor and recognition. It occurs 11 times in this LXX corpus, across books including Job, Isaiah, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage says about the person or thing being described.

word:lxx:L702161.explanation: This adverb means “on the spot,” referring to a place where something happens or to action taken immediately at that location. It points to what occurs right there, rather than elsewhere or at a later time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears five times, including once in Joshua and four times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a sentence depends on whether it describes a location, an immediate response, or an event occurring directly at that place.

word:lxx:L702284.explanation: Achimōth is a proper name, rendered as “Achimōth” or “Akhimoth.” It identifies a named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 6:10. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise genealogical role cannot be stated here, but its lexical function is clear: it is a personal name.

word:lxx:L702330.explanation: This word means “2; beth.” It functions as an unchanging numerical designation, identifying the second position or item, while also naming beth. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:9. Because the available meaning is brief and the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that heading or passage must be understood from its surrounding context. Its basic sense remains a marker for the second entry, associated with beth.

word:lxx:L702349.explanation: Baani is a personal name, also represented as Vaani. It identifies an individual rather than describing an object, action, quality, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 8:10. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its use as a person’s name in that one recorded occurrence.

word:lxx:L702455.explanation: Baiōn, also rendered Veon, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Septuagint tradition, so its significance comes from what is being named in each passage, not from an abstract idea built into the word itself. It occurs three times in the LXX corpus: twice in Joshua and once in 1 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines the specific referent.

word:lxx:L702503.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered as “Banaibakat” or “Vanevakat.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Because proper names normally identify people or places rather than translate into an ordinary descriptive meaning, its significance depends on the surrounding passage and the entity it names. word:lxx:L702576.explanation: “Basi” is a proper name, also identified as “Vasi.” It refers to a person named in the Greek Old Testament text, rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, the name’s specific role in that listing should be understood from Ezra 2:49 itself.

word:lxx:L702617.explanation: This noun means a “breach”—a break, opening, or damaged place in something that should be whole or secure. In this Greek Old Testament usage, the word appears nine times, all in 2 Kings, where it is associated with breaches requiring attention and repair. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a damaged opening or break.

word:lxx:L702680.explanation: This word is a proper name, preserved in English as “Bēthanathinim” or “Vithanathinim.” It does not describe an action, quality, or ordinary object; it identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:31. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its particular referent cannot be explained further here, but its lexical function is that of a name rather than a general description.

word:lxx:L702778.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Boubastos” or “Vuvastos.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L702806.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “slow”: to delay, move slowly, or take longer than expected. It describes slowness as an action or process rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it appears four times, spread across Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what or who is being described as slow, but the central idea remains delayed or unhurried action.

word:lxx:L702954.explanation: Gamzō is the name of a place.

word:lxx:L703005.explanation: Geth is a proper name for a place.

word:lxx:L703157.explanation: Gothoniel is a personal name, rendered as “Gothoniēl” or “Gothonil.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs eight times across seven verses, appearing in Joshua, Judges, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and account, but the word itself functions as a proper name for a person.

word:lxx:L703272.explanation: Daman, also rendered Thaman, is a proper name. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Jeremiah 47:1. The available lexical meaning identifies it as a name rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the exact person, place, or reference intended at that point cannot be clarified from the word alone. word:lxx:L703351.explanation: Delphōn is a personal name, rendered in English as Delphon.

Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be described further; its lexical meaning remains clear.

word:lxx:L703508.explanation: Dialysis means separating one from another.

word:lxx:L703614.explanation: This verb means “run across,” describing movement quickly from one side or place to another. It is an action word, so it portrays someone or something traveling across a space rather than merely remaining in motionless presence. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs four times, in three Old Testament passages and once in Wisdom. The surrounding verse determines what is being crossed and why, but the central idea remains movement across a space.

word:lxx:L703733.explanation: Diospolis, also rendered Thiospolis, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel: 30:14 and 30:16. The name itself identifies the location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical function is simply to name Diospolis.

word:lxx:L703746.explanation: This adjective means “two-edged,” describing something made sharp or effective on both sides. It is used of an object or image whose two edges can cut, rather than of a one-sided blade. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Judges, Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the noun or image it describes.

word:lxx:L703852.explanation: This adjective describes something that is hard to escape or inescapable. It can characterize a situation, condition, or thing from which escape is difficult or impossible. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:16, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its central sense remains clear: what cannot easily be escaped. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L703975.explanation: This verb means to have cravings—to experience a strong desire for something. It describes an inward appetite or longing rather than a simple action of taking or receiving. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in three verses in Genesis. Its occurrences belong to the language of desire connected with animals and their breeding, but the word itself chiefly expresses the experience of craving. The surrounding verse determines precisely what is desired and how that desire functions in the sentence.

word:lxx:L704031.explanation: Eder, also given as Ether, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a designation rather than a general description or action word. This name occurs two times in the LXX, both in 1 Chronicles: 23:23 and 24:30. The available wording preserves the name itself, but without the surrounding verse text, it does not establish whether the named individual or group is being identified in either passage.

word:lxx:L704093.explanation: Eimi means be. It is rendered as “art” in a statement identifying someone.

word:lxx:L704237.explanation: Ekleipō means to leave off or cease.

word:lxx:L704318.explanation: This verb means “sweep away,” describing the act of removing or carrying something off. It presents movement that clears something from its place rather than merely touching or moving it slightly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 5:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on sweeping something away or making it disappear from where it stood.

word:lxx:L704804.explanation: Entos means inside, referring to what is within something.

word:lxx:L704985.explanation: This verb means “drive,” describing the act of forcing or moving someone or something away. It presents action rather than a person, place, or quality. word:lxx:L705003.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “ashamed”: it describes experiencing or expressing shame. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. word:lxx:L705076.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “fix on; hold on.” It describes directing attention toward something or maintaining a firm hold, depending on how it functions in its sentence. word:lxx:L705155.explanation: This verb means “conceal”: to hide something from view or keep it from being openly seen. word:lxx:L705278.explanation: Epistrephō means to turn around or return.

word:lxx:L705317.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “manifest”: to make something known, clear, or visible. It describes something being brought into view or made plainly recognizable. word:lxx:L705380.explanation: This verb expresses love, including being filled with passion. word:lxx:L705461.explanation: Esabana, also rendered Esavana, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L705528.explanation: This Greek LXX verb refers to a comrade or to comrade-like association. word:lxx:L705595.explanation: This noun means “prosperity”—a condition of flourishing, abundance, or material well-being. It describes favorable plenty rather than a person, action, or command. word:lxx:L705630.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “sweetly-speaking”—using speech that is pleasant, gentle, or appealing to hear. word:lxx:L705649.explanation: This noun means “good order” or “order”—a condition in which things are arranged properly and function in an orderly way. word:lxx:L705784.explanation: Echran is a proper name, rendered “Echran” and also given as “Ekhran.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L706235.explanation: This adjective means “female” or “of women.” It identifies someone or something as belonging to the female sex and functions as a describing word rather than a name or action. word:lxx:L706323.explanation: This Greek noun means “tempest,” referring to a powerful storm or turbulent wind. It names a weather disturbance rather than an action or quality. word:lxx:L706381.explanation: Iazēl, also rendered “Iazil,” is a proper name rather than a descriptive word.
